html:
This is how I run DeepSeek's October 17 release of V4.1 Flash as one engine across four GB10 machines: the exact checkpoint, the image, every flag, the storage and kernel settings that mattered, the measured speeds, and the tests behind them. It is written so you can rebuild it. Where my setup has a machine name, an address, a port or a key, this page has a placeholder in angle brackets.

The short version: the published four-GB10 recipe got me running at the speeds its author reported, and two changes made it about 25% faster per decode step on real agentic coding work. One was a storage setting on the server that holds the weights. The other was turning on part of vLLM's kernel autotuning, after the full autotune deadlocked.

What runs

PartWhat I used
Modeldeepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017: 40 layers, 384 routed experts (6 active per token) plus 1 shared expert, two Engram n-gram tables (layers 1 and 14), its own speculative drafter (DSpark)
CheckpointLibertAIDAI/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4 at revision 5be99cd15675589fb6693d0a8651e413bcb9a396: 48 shards, 399.5 GiB
Quantizationrouted experts NVFP4 W4A4 (a bit-exact transcode of the MXFP4 originals); Engram tables MXFP4 (lossy: cosine 0.9934 against the FP8 source); everything else as released
Machinestwo ASUS Ascent GX10 and two Gigabyte AI TOP ATOM (all GB10: 20 Arm cores, 128 GB LPDDR5X shared by CPU and GPU)
Networkone ConnectX-7 port per box into one switch, RoCE v2, MTU 9000
Host softwareNVIDIA driver 580.178.04, Docker 29.6 with GPU access; everything else is inside the image
EnginevLLM nightly 0.30.1rc1.dev558 (commit 0cbac6cd1) plus nine Python-only patches
Layouttensor-parallel 4: one process per box, vLLM's own multiprocessing launcher (no Ray)
Window1,048,576 tokens; the KV pool holds 2,508,742 tokens (8 GiB per box)
Speculative decodingDSpark, 5 draft tokens per step
APIOpenAI-compatible, on node 0, behind an API key

The measured result

All numbers are from 2026-10-24, sampling at temperature 1.0 and top_p 1.0 (what the model card asks for; lower temperatures make this model loop in its reasoning).

TestResult
Decode step at 32K / 100K / 180K tokens of context62.0 / 60.7 / 60.5 ms
Decode speed in that test58.8 / 73.0 / 71.8 tok/s (tokens per step varies with what it is writing)
Agent loop, thinking on, 3 rounds, engine totals71.3 tok/s, 60.5 ms per step, 4.32 tokens per step; 3/3 rounds pass
Time to first token on a turn whose prompt is cached0.44–0.51 s
Prefill of text the model has not seen before2.5–3.0K tok/s (10.6 s for a fresh 30K-token prompt)
Boot, launch to first answer4–6 minutes

How each of these was measured is in How I measured. For comparison, the published recipe I started from reports 65–67 tok/s for single-stream code; my first boot measured 67.3 tok/s on the same kind of test, before either change below.

1. Hardware and network

  • Four GB10 machines. Mixed vendors are fine; mine are two ASUS Ascent GX10 and two Gigabyte AI TOP ATOM. Each has 128 GB of memory that the CPU and the GPU share (122 GiB visible to Linux). That sharing matters twice below: the KV cache is set in bytes, not as a share of GPU memory, and anything that allocates GPU memory also squeezes the Linux page cache.
  • One network. One ConnectX-7 port per machine into one switch, MTU 9000, RoCE v2. GB10 shows that port as two RDMA devices (two PCIe halves); NCCL uses both (rocep1s0f1 and roceP2p1s0f1 on mine; ls /sys/class/infiniband lists yours). Keep this network to these machines only: vLLM's traffic between ranks is not authenticated.
  • The RoCE v2 IPv4 GID is index 3 on all four of mine. Check yours with show_gids or cat /sys/class/infiniband/<dev>/ports/1/gid_attrs/types/*.
  • A separate storage server exports the model folder over NFS (NFS over RDMA in my case), and every GB10 mounts it read-only at the same path. I use /srv/models on this page.
  • Cooling. Node 0 (the one serving the API) runs hottest, because it also runs vLLM's API server and engine core. Under sustained decode its SoC reached 85–89 °C, and several times it touched 90–91 °C. Benchmarks here run under a watchdog that stops them at GPU 82 °C or SoC 90 °C; the other three boxes stayed at 65–80 °C. Idle, node 0 sits at 45–50 °C.

2. The weights

Download only what vLLM needs. The repository also carries Python scripts (DeepSeek's reference inference code and the quantizer's conversion scripts); vLLM needs none of them, and this setup never passes --trust-remote-code.

HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1 hf download LibertAIDAI/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4 \
  --revision 5be99cd15675589fb6693d0a8651e413bcb9a396 \
  --cache-dir /srv/models/hub --max-workers 2 \
  --include '*.safetensors' --include config.json --include hf_quant_config.json \
  --include model.safetensors.index.json --include tokenizer.json --include tokenizer_config.json \
  --include LICENSE --include README.md

Two traps:

  • xet off, two workers. With xet on, huggingface_hub 2.x assembles whole files in RAM. With 52 GB shards that means tens of GB of RAM per worker.
  • Shards 47 and 48 refuse to download without xet. They are 52.4 GB each: the two Engram tables. hf 2.2.0 stops with "The file is too large to be downloaded using the regular download method". I fetched those two with resumable HTTP range requests from the Hub's resolve URL, then checked each file's sha256 against its LFS id before linking it into the snapshot:
url=https://huggingface.co/LibertAIDAI/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4/resolve/5be99cd15675589fb6693d0a8651e413bcb9a396/model-00047-of-00048.safetensors
until curl -fL --retry 5 -C - -o model-00047.part "$url"; do sleep 10; done
sha256sum model-00047.part   # must equal the LFS oid the Hub lists for this file

Then prove the whole snapshot matches the Hub byte for byte: the sha256 of all 48 shards against their LFS ids, and the git blob sha1 of the small files. Mine passed with 55 files checked, 0 problems.

Put the Engram shards on small records

If the share is ZFS, do this now. It was the biggest fix in this whole recipe (section 6 tells the story).

The engine reads Engram rows, 136 bytes each at random offsets, straight from those two shard files on every step. A dataset with recordsize=1M makes every 4 KB read cost a full 1 MiB record. Rewrite just those two files with 16 KiB records and leave the rest of the dataset as it was. ZFS fixes a file's block size when the file is written, so:

sudo zfs set recordsize=16K <pool>/<dataset>
for blob in <sha256-of-shard-47> <sha256-of-shard-48>; do        # blob names under hub/.../blobs/
  dd if="$blob" of="$blob.16k" bs=16M iflag=fullblock conv=fsync status=none
  [ "$(sha256sum < "$blob.16k" | cut -d' ' -f1)" = "$blob" ] && mv -f "$blob.16k" "$blob"
done
sudo zfs set recordsize=1M <pool>/<dataset>
stat -c %o <blob>    # ZFS reports the file's record size here: 16384 afterwards

Use dd, not cp. On a pool with block cloning (OpenZFS 2.2+ with feature@block_cloning active), cp's copy_file_range clones the old 1 MiB blocks instead of rewriting them, and nothing changes. Do the rewrite with the engine stopped: the ranks memory-map these files over NFS, and swapping a file under them leaves stale file handles.

3. The image

Base: the vLLM nightly for commit 0cbac6cd1, pinned by digest: vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:8e6e3752946ff2dde451b313cbaec2ea8e7b52221b21bfbcf53fb68dd4f4c42e (a multi-arch manifest; the GB10s use its arm64 image).

Patches: nine, all Python, applied with zero fuzz. They are the set from calvarado2004/deepseek-v41-1017-nvfp4 at 8f57fb8 (the published four-GB10 recipe this one starts from), unchanged:

PatchWhat it doesOrigin
0001Engram rows read from the checkpoint file each step (--engram-config {"disk_offload": true})ondigo-winder
0002V4.1 on sm_12x: per-layer KV page sizes, a null-block fix, the DSpark drafter's experts on MXFP4ondigo-winder
0003MXFP4 Engram tables (this checkpoint), widened to E4M3 on the GPU. Only works through 0001's disk pathondigo-winder
0004the V4.1 encoder synced with the 1017 reference (Python part of vllm#62196)vLLM
0005DeepGEMM: restore SM12x contiguous-layout alignment 64 (vllm#58681)vLLM
0006draft_context_window for DSpark (vllm#61261)vLLM
0007fresh random draws across block-verification rounds (vllm#61161)vLLM
0008skip bonus-logit reductions for short drafts (vllm#61451)vLLM
0009V4.1 image order follows rendered content (vllm#60792)vLLM

I skipped that recipe's 0010 (a faster InstantTensor loader). Before using any of them I read every hunk: they only open checkpoint files read-only, and they add no subprocess, network, eval or pickle calls.

Why this nightly and not the v0.32.0 release: on v0.32.0 the patch set leaves seven hunks to merge by hand, including 0001's Engram reader, whose lookup-kernel call changed signature. A mistake there corrupts output without an error. On this nightly all nine apply cleanly.

Build without running anything. Because the patches are pure Python, the image needs no RUN step:

  1. List the files the patches touch (+++ b/... lines).
  2. Copy each original out of the base with docker create and docker cp, so nothing in the image runs.
  3. Apply the patches with patch -p1 --fuzz=0. Any reject stops the build.
  4. Byte-compile the patched files with the image's own Python 3.12, in a container with --network none.
  5. COPY the result over the installed package.
FROM vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:8e6e3752946ff2dde451b313cbaec2ea8e7b52221b21bfbcf53fb68dd4f4c42e
COPY vllm/ /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/
COPY no-merge.jinja /opt/recipe/no-merge.jinja

no-merge.jinja is one line, {% for m in messages %}{{ m['content'] }}{% endfor %}. DeepSeek ships no Jinja template, and the V4.1 tokenizer mode builds the prompt itself, but vLLM still wants a template file. The line and that reason come from the reference recipe's launcher.

With no RUN steps, one docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --network none works on an x86 box without QEMU. Building on one GB10 works too. Export the arm64 image with docker save, put the tar and its sha256 on the share, and on every GB10 check the sha256 before docker load. Every rank must run byte-identical Python: compare the sha256 of the patched files across nodes before the first boot.

4. Launch

One container per machine, the same image, the same flags; only the node rank differs. Start nodes 3, 2 and 1 first, then node 0, which also serves the API.

docker run -d --name dsv41-r<RANK> \
  --gpus all --network host --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  --device /dev/infiniband --cap-add IPC_LOCK \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 --ulimit nofile=1048576:1048576 \
  -v /srv/models:/srv/models:ro -v /srv/vllm-cache:/cache \
  -e VLLM_HOST_IP=<THIS_NODE_FABRIC_IP> \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME==<FABRIC_NETDEV> -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=<FABRIC_NETDEV> \
  -e NCCL_IB_HCA==rocep1s0f1,roceP2p1s0f1 \
  -e NCCL_NET=IB -e NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 -e NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=none \
  -e NCCL_IB_ROCE_VERSION_NUM=2 -e NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3 \
  -e NCCL_IB_MERGE_NICS=0 -e NCCL_CROSS_NIC=0 -e NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=0 -e NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0 \
  -e NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS=8 \
  -e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 -e TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 -e HF_HUB_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 \
  -e VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1 -e DO_NOT_TRACK=1 \
  -e VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn -e VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 \
  -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True -e VLLM_SAFETENSORS_CLONE_ON_LOAD=1 \
  -e HOME=/cache -e HF_HOME=/cache/hf -e XDG_CACHE_HOME=/cache -e VLLM_CACHE_ROOT=/cache/vllm \
  -e TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/cache/triton -e TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/cache/inductor -e CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/cache/nv \
  -e FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE=/cache/fi -e VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_CACHE_DIR=/cache/fi-autotune \
  -e VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS=mxfp8_gemm,trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1,trtllm::fused_moe::gemm2 \
  --entrypoint vllm <IMAGE> serve /srv/models/hub/models--LibertAIDAI--DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4/snapshots/5be99cd15675589fb6693d0a8651e413bcb9a396 \
  --served-model-name deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 \
  --distributed-executor-backend mp --nnodes 4 --node-rank <RANK> \
  --master-addr <NODE0_FABRIC_IP> --master-port <MASTER_PORT> \
  --max-model-len 1048576 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 8589934592 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --language-model-only --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
  --chat-template /opt/recipe/no-merge.jinja \
  --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune": true}' \
  --engram-config '{"disk_offload": true, "disk_offload_threads": 64}' \
  --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype": "mxfp4"}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 5, "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic", "rejection_sample_method": "block", "enable_adaptive_verification": false, "draft_context_window": 32768}' \
  --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --override-generation-config '{"temperature": 1.0, "top_p": 1.0}' \
  <ON NODE 0: --host <NODE0_FABRIC_IP> --port <PORT> and --env-file <file holding VLLM_API_KEY=...>>
  <ON NODES 1-3: --headless>

Why these values:

  • --kv-cache-memory-bytes 8589934592 (8 GiB): set the KV pool in bytes. With it set, vLLM skips its memory profiling and --gpu-memory-utilization only gates start-up, which is what you want when CPU and GPU share one pool. 8 GiB per rank gives 2,508,742 tokens: 2.39 full 1M-token requests.
  • **--engram-config with disk_offload**: at tensor-parallel 4 the MXFP4 Engram tables do not fit beside 77.6 GiB of weights per rank. Rows are read from the shard files through the page cache instead. With this checkpoint it is also the only path patch 0003 supports.
  • --attention-config {"indexer_kv_dtype": "mxfp4"}: the sparse-attention indexer's K cache in MXFP4 instead of FP8, which grows the KV pool (about 40% on GB10, per the reference recipe; sm_12x only).
  • --language-model-only: text only. Image and URL inputs are off.
  • --override-generation-config: the model card's sampling becomes the server default, so clients that send nothing still get temperature 1.0 and top_p 1.0.
  • NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS=8: GB10 has no GPUDirect RDMA, so each NCCL connection pins about 9 MiB of host memory for the NIC. Eight channels keeps that to about 2.7 GiB per node.
  • **--kernel-config autotune plus the skip list**: see section 7. Leave the skip list out and the boot can hang.

Ready check. The first boot takes 4–6 minutes: about 3.5 minutes of weight loading over NFS (target model, then the drafter), JIT kernel warmup, then CUDA-graph capture. /health answering 200 does not prove the peers are alive, so prove the engine with a real completion:

curl -s http://<NODE0_FABRIC_IP>:<PORT>/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017", "max_tokens": 64,
       "chat_template_kwargs": {"thinking": false},
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17*23? Answer with just the number."}]}'
# expect "content": "391", finish_reason "stop"

5. Using it

  • Thinking is on by default. Send "chat_template_kwargs": {"thinking": false} on /v1/chat/completions to turn it off for a request. With thinking on, give max_tokens room (4096 or more), or a short cap returns empty content.
  • **When streaming, the thinking arrives in a delta field named reasoning**, not reasoning_content. A client or benchmark that ignores it times the first answer token instead of the first token, and over-counts decode speed.
  • Tool calls work with the deepseek_v41 parser and come back with finish_reason: "tool_calls".
  • Expect the first few minutes after any restart to be slower. Loading ~78 GB of weights through the page cache pushes the Engram rows out. My first agent run after a boot measured 58–65 tok/s; later runs measured about 71.

6. The fix that mattered most: Engram on small records

How I found it. I ran the lane on a normal agentic-coding session with opencode (about 100 requests) and read vLLM's own Prometheus metrics afterwards:

  • Prompts were big: a median of 108K tokens, p90 182K, but 98% of prompt tokens came from the prefix cache.
  • Decode was nearly all the time: 89% of request time (1,198 of 1,342 s), prefill 10%, queueing 0.
  • The step rate: ~79 ms per decode step, 3.9 tokens per step, so ~49 tok/s.
  • Draft acceptance by position: 85 / 70 / 56 / 45 / 35%.

So decode step time was the target. A sweep showed it did not depend on context length (78 / 78 / 77 / 82 ms at 2K / 32K / 100K / 180K), which pointed at fixed per-step costs.

Then one request with about 326K tokens of context and new content took 8 minutes 40 seconds to prefill. The evidence during that stall:

  • one GB10 sat at 61% iowait with its GPU idle, while two others spun at 96% "utilization" (really NCCL waiting for it);
  • the storage server answered ~97 MB/s of NFS reads while its pool read 1.5 GB/s from the drives.

Why. The dataset holding the model had recordsize=1M and primarycache=metadata, settings that are right for streaming 400 GB of weights. Engram rows are tiny and random, and the engine gathers them before every step. Each rank maps ~47 GiB of rows, but the page cache beside the weights holds only ~13–17 GiB. New n-grams keep landing on rows that aren't cached, and every miss cost a full 1 MiB read on the server. During the normal session the server answered 400–4,000 NFS reads per second, about 130–170 per decode step.

I made the stall worse myself: an NCCL benchmark I had just run allocated GPU memory, which on GB10 is page-cache memory, and evicted the warm rows.

The change: the two Engram shards on 16 KiB records (section 2). Measured right after a restart, with every row cold:

Test1 MiB records16 KiB records
Time to first token, fresh prompt 32K / 100K / 180K19.6 / 36.2 / 49.9 s12.2 / 20.2 / 25.4 s
Prefill of new text1.5–1.7K tok/s2.5–3.0K tok/s
Agent loop, thinking on (decode median)59.0 tok/s63.8 tok/s

With vLLM's VLLM_ENGRAM_TIMING=1 log, a decode step now spends ~1.0–1.5 ms per table gathering 36–40 rows per rank. That is about 3 ms of a step. So this fixed prefill and the stalls, but it did not explain the rest of the 75 ms.

7. The second fix: decode-only FlashInfer autotune

Profile first. vLLM's torch profiler (--profiler-config '{"profiler": "torch", "torch_profiler_dir": "...", "delay_iterations": 5, "max_iterations": 40}', then POST /start_profile, one request, POST /stop_profile) captured 40 decode steps on every rank. Every rank did the same GPU work, about 72 ms per step:

Kernel familyPer step
MXFP8 dense GEMMs (DeviceGemmMxfp8GemmSm120, ~5.7 per layer)25.8 ms: 229 calls × 112 µs
MoE grouped GEMMs23.2 ms: 80 calls × 290 µs, close to GB10's memory bandwidth already
BF16 GEMMs on old SM80 WMMA kernels~9.5 ms
attention + indexer, norms, Engram, sampling~6 ms

By my estimate the MXFP8 GEMMs ran 6–7× slower than just reading their weights would take: each call gets a 6-row input (one verify step), and the default kernel used a 128 × 32 × 128 tile. Picking the right kernel variant for a shape is what FlashInfer's autotuner does. It was off, because the configuration I started from disables it.

The full autotune deadlocked. With enable_flashinfer_autotune: true vLLM runs two passes.

  1. A decode-sized pass. Rank 0 tunes alone and broadcasts the result; it tuned mxfp8_gemm and the fused-MoE GEMMs and saved 77 configs.
  2. A prefill-sized pass. All ranks tune in lockstep over a CPU process group. At the end of this one, rank 0 sat in an NCCL kernel while the other three waited on the CPU group, for good.

That was not slow storage: the server served zero NFS reads and the GB10s showed no iowait.

The workaround. vLLM has a skip list for the second pass, VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS. Listing the three ops the first pass already tuned (mxfp8_gemm, trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1, trtllm::fused_moe::gemm2) makes the second pass finish in about 6 seconds, and the decode configs stay loaded on every rank. The cache lives in VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_CACHE_DIR, so later boots reuse it. Prefill keeps the default tactics. If a newer image hangs after "Running FlashInfer autotune", add the op it was tuning to the list.

The result, measured the same way before and after:

TestEngram fix only+ decode autotune
MXFP8 GEMM per call112 µs51 µs
Decode step at 32K / 100K / 180K74.1 / 71.6 / 87.5 ms62.0 / 60.7 / 60.5 ms
The same profiled 400-token request24.1 s15.2 s
Agent loop, thinking on (decode median)63.8 tok/s78.9 tok/s with warm rows

From this morning's 77–82 ms per decode step to ~61 ms: about 25% less time per step.

8. What did not help

All measured, all reverted.

TriedResult
7 draft tokens (the reference recipe's choice)Same agent-loop speed as 5 (68.1 vs 69.3 tok/s) and node 0 hit SoC 90–91 °C
6 draft tokens, after the autotune69.0 ms per step at 32K for 3.89 tokens (5 drafts: 62.0 ms for 3.65), and node 0 hit 90 °C
4 draft tokens69.4 tok/s against 71.3 with 5 (agent loop, engine totals). On real sessions, dropping a draft costs ~9% of tokens to save ~4% of time
KV pool 4 GiB instead of 8 (4 GiB more page cache per node)No measurable change: 69.5 vs 71.3 tok/s, same NFS traffic. New text keeps hitting rows it has never seen
NCCL tuningAlready near its floor: ~76 µs per decode-size all-reduce across four nodes, ~9 ms of a step. NCCL_PROTO=LL was no faster, one RDMA device instead of two the same, and NCCL_ALGO=Tree is refused ("invalid usage")
cuBLASLt for the BF16 GEMMs (TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_CUBLASLT=1)Identical to cuBLAS on these shapes in a microbenchmark
torch.compileOff by design for this model: vLLM runs it with breakable CUDA graphs and its own fused kernels

What is left needs code, not settings: small-M kernels (or FP8 weights) for the BF16 projections, and tuned tactics for prefill once the lockstep autotune stops deadlocking.

How I measured

Every benchmark ran under a watchdog that sampled all four machines every 5 seconds and stopped the run at GPU 82 °C or SoC 90 °C. The numbers come from vLLM's own counters, so client overhead is not in them.

  • Real use: the counters on node 0's /metrics over the session window.
    • Decode vs prefill time: vllm:request_decode_time_seconds_sum and vllm:request_prefill_time_seconds_sum.
    • Steps: vllm:spec_decode_num_drafts_total, one per verify step.
    • Acceptance: vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_per_pos_total.
    • Prefix-cache hits: vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total over vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total.
  • Context sweep: one instruction ("list the files above, one line each") after 2K, 32K, 100K and 180K tokens of source code, thinking off, 700 output tokens, one request at a time. Per request: decode seconds ÷ verify steps from the counter deltas = ms per step.
  • Agent loop: a scripted coding task against a small generated repository: read two files (parallel tool calls), write the fix, run the tests, summarize. Thinking on, 3 rounds after a warm-up run, every tool call answered. A round passes only if the fix is correct and the tests ran after it. Reported as engine totals (tokens ÷ decode seconds), which is steadier than a per-turn median.
  • Profiles: vLLM's torch profiler as in section 7, then GPU time per kernel name per step from the trace.
  • NCCL: a torch.distributed all-reduce benchmark on the same four ranks, image and NCCL settings, median of 200 calls per size. A 20-call run read 180–200 µs because its median still included connection warm-up.

How I got here

  1. Start from the published recipe. The four-GB10 card from calvarado2004 (built on ondigo-winder's patches) is a published, measured vLLM configuration for this exact checkpoint on GB10. I pinned the same base, the same patches and most of its settings, and my first boot matched its reported speed (67.3 vs 65–67 tok/s single-stream code). Differences: weights on a network share instead of local NVMe, stock NCCL through a switch instead of a switchless ring, the stock model loader, and no --trust-remote-code.
  2. Tune for my traffic. I kept 5 drafts instead of 7: the same speed in my agent loop, and less heat on node 0.
  3. Measure real use, not just benchmarks. One working session showed decode was 89% of the time, and that step time did not depend on context. That ruled out attention and pointed at fixed per-step costs.
  4. Chase the stall. iowait on one node, NCCL spin on the others and the server's drive throughput pointed at the storage. The record size explained it.
  5. Profile before guessing. The per-kernel profile showed one kernel family 6–7× off its bandwidth limit, and that is the kind of problem an autotuner fixes.
  6. When the autotune hung, find out where. Two passes; only the second deadlocks; vLLM already had the skip list. My first reaction had been to write autotune off. It was worth the second look.
  7. Try the cheap ideas too, and keep only what measures. Draft count, KV size, NCCL settings and BLAS backend all came back flat (section 8).

Security notes

  • Keep the inter-node network private to these machines. vLLM's traffic between ranks (its TCP store, ZMQ and NCCL) is not authenticated.
  • Put the API behind a key (VLLM_API_KEY from an env file, not on the command line), bind it to the private address only, and put a router or gateway in front if anything else needs it.
  • Run offline: HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 and the telemetry switches above. The weights are read-only on every node.
  • Never pass --trust-remote-code for this checkpoint, and do not download the repository's Python files; vLLM needs neither.
  • Read the patches before you build. They change the engine's Python, and you are running them as root inside a container with host networking.
